question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: The ensemble suggests a very high probability (96%) of raising the default settlement qualifying period to 10 years under the Earned Settlement framework, with reductions possible for those contributing.
Adversarial objections flag potential legislative delays, transitional rules, and political pushback that could impede a universal 10-year baseline by May 2026.
Long-residence already operates on a 10-year baseline, providing precedent and feasibility for a 10-year default, supporting momentum.
Overall, momentum is strong, but near-term realization by May 2026 is not guaranteed; a calibrated probability around the low-to-mid 90s best captures the balance of signals and risks.

justification.critique_assessment: The objections are valid and identify credible timing and rollout risks that could delay universal adoption, warranting a modest downward adjustment from the ensemble.
justification.adjustment: Adjusted probability from 0.96 to 0.92 to reflect plausible legislative timing delays and transitional rollout complexities; no downward adjustment due to physically implausible scenarios was necessary.

forecasts.reference-class: UK government settlement policy reforms (earned settlement) moving from a 5-year baseline to a 10-year baseline for the qualifying period, with reductions for contributions; status as of early 2026 indicates formal proposals and consultation completed or near completion.

sources.claim: The government announced a proposed new contribution-based settlement model that requires a minimum of 10 years lawful residence to settle, doubling the current period.

The government said it would double the permanent settlement qualifying period for migrants to 10 years, with reductions for those contributing, applying to migrants arriving from 2021 (subject to transitional arrangements).
The Earned Settlement consultation states that the default qualifying period for settlement will be increased to 10 years, with potential reductions based on contribution.
The immigration rules outline the long-residence and other routes to settlement, providing context for the evolving 10-year baseline in the policy reform discussions.

House of Commons Library briefing notes that changes to visa and settlement rules are under consultation with a target of increasing the baseline qualifying period to 10 years, with a consultation running into February 2026.
Long residence already requires 10 years of continuous lawful residence to qualify for settlement, illustrating the 10-year baseline concept in practice for at least one route.
The default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from 5 years to 10 years, with exceptions.
Baseline 10-year period for most earned settlement; other categories have longer periods (15/20/30) and adjustments.
Home Office announced a major consultation to increase the settlement qualifying period, with details about 10-year baselines and potential changes.
Proposed time-adjustment model with 10-year baseline for most routes; 15/20 years for other categories.
Long residence route requires 10 years continuous lawful residence; current framework anchors around 10 years.
10-year qualifying period under continuous residence guidance; time counts from various routes toward settlement.
IPPR warns that changes could extend settlement timelines to 10 or more years for many migrants, affecting children.
Critics warn that earned settlement could delay dependants' access to settlement and welfare rights.
Oxford Migration Observatory analysis questions the social and economic impact of extended settlement timelines.
The government states that settlement will move from 5 years to 10 years, with earned adjustments.
The Earned Settlement consultation outlines a default 10-year qualifying period with reductions for contributions and increases for negative factors.
Immigration Rules document discusses the framework for settlement and continuous residence rules.
Electronic Immigration Network reports the proposal to double the ILR qualifying period to 10 years with a timeline for April 2026 implementation.
Hill Dickinson notes the consultation closing Feb 12, 2026 and that the proposal would abolish the 10-year long residence route; 10-year baseline with possible reductions.
Guardian reports the government’s white paper proposing extending the settlement wait to 10 years.
